study. In summary, this multimodal dataset comprises 143 data points 
characterized by 47 predictor variables, as detailed in Table 1. These 
data are expected to provide key information for the accurate analysis 
and estimation of SOC levels in the Beja district, thereby supporting the 
objectives of the present study.

Learning from limited and heterogeneous data is a crucial capability 
in domains where data acquisition is costly or logistically constrained. 
Under these conditions, models must derive robust and generalizable 
patterns from sparse, noisy, and diverse information sources. This set-
ting poses a demanding benchmark for any learning approach, reveal-
ing its capacity to develop data-efficient, resilient, and context-aware 
intelligence.

For this study, satellite images were obtained through the Google 
Earth Engine Plataform.3 These images provided average spectral data 
corresponding to the annual recordings from the Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, 
and Sentinel-3 satellites. Additionally, topographic characteristics were 
accessed using data from the Copernicus DEM satellite.4 Futhermore, 
satellite images related to the annual average precipitation and tem-
perature were used, sourced from the Climatic Research Unit (CRU) 
databases for the year 2018.5 Climate variables derived from CRU were 
used at their native spatial support (approximately 1 km) and provide 
regional-scale context, whereas terrain and remote-sensing predictors

capture fine-scale spatial variability at 30 m resolution. For non-graph-
based methods, two additional features—latitude and longitude of 
SOC sampling locations—were included to capture geographical spatial 
patterns in the dataset. All bands of these images were used as predic-
tor variables to estimate SOC. Fig. 2 illustrates practical examples of 
visualizing Sentinel-1, -2, -3 bands.

Next subsections describe the data sources of the SOC predictors 
listed in Table 1, maintaining alignment between predictors and data 
modalities. The satellite image data used in this study have varying 
native spatial resolutions, as shown in Table 1. For example, Sentinel-2 
spectral bands (B1–B12) are provided at 10 m, 20 m, or 60 m resolution 
depending on the band, with the QA60 cloud mask originally at 60 m. 
For consistency in the analysis, bands with coarser resolutions were 
optionally resampled to 30 m where appropriate, using interpolation 
methods to better align with higher-resolution layers. Sentinel-3 OLCI 
bands (Oa01–Oa21) have an original spatial resolution of approxi-
mately 300 m and were not directly acquired at 30 m; when included in 
analyses requiring a finer spatial scale, these bands were either used at 
their native resolution or resampled as needed. This approach balances 
spatial detail preservation and data integration requirements, avoiding 
unnecessary resampling when not required for the specific analysis.

This dataset poses significant challenges for machine learning mod-
els. The small sample size limits generalization and increases the risk 
of overfitting, while the relatively high dimensionality complicates 
effective feature-space exploration. Moreover, the strong heterogeneity 
among variables, stemming from diverse geospatial, environmental, 
and contextual sources, introduces complex, non-linear relationships 
that conventional models struggle to capture. Together, these factors 
make robust learning and inference particularly difficult, yet they also

2.2.1. SOC data

The SOC data used in this study were obtained from two reputable 
sources: the European Soil Data Centre (ESDAC)6 and the International 
Soil Reference and Information Centre (ISRIC)7 for the year 2018. SOC 
data consist of soil samples collected and analyzed according to the 
standards of the International Soil Organization (ISO). Each soil sample 
is georeferenced with precise latitude and longitude coordinates and 
includes information on soil profile depth, specifically SOC measure-
ments within the 0–40 cm depth range. A total of 143 georeferenced 
soil samples were collected within the Beja district, providing detailed 
information on organic carbon content and their exact spatial locations 
as shown in Fig. 3.

The geospatial coordinates of these samples act as a pivotal link, 
enabling the extraction and integration of diverse environmental and 
spatial features from the sources listed in Table 1, while ensuring their 
spatio-temporal alignment with SOC measurements. Although the satel-
lite imagery covers a large area of thousands of square kilometers, each 
coordinate allows the identification of the exact pixel corresponding to 
the SOC sampling location.

To examine the distribution of SOC values, Fig. 4(a) presents a 
histogram showing right skewness, with a concentration of lower values 
and a long tail toward higher values (outliers). To address this issue 
and improve the data’s suitability for predictive modeling, a natural 
logarithmic transformation (LN(SOC)) was applied. This transformation 
effectively reduces the skewness, leading to a close-to-normal distribu-
tion, as show in Fig. 4(b), which helps mitigate the influence of outliers 
and stabilize variance.

2.2.2. Global and local spatial autocorrelation of SOC

Global spatial autocorrelation of SOC was assessed using Moran’s 
𝐼 statistic to evaluate whether SOC values exhibit systematic spatial 
dependence across the study area. Moran’s 𝐼 measures the degree of 
similarity among observations as a function of spatial proximity and is 
defined as

where 𝑛 denotes the number of sampling locations, 𝑥𝑖 and 𝑥𝑗 are SOC 
values at locations 𝑖 and 𝑗, respectively, ̄𝑥 is the mean SOC value, 𝑤𝑖𝑗
represents the spatial weight between locations 𝑖 and 𝑗, and 𝑆0 is the 
sum of all spatial weights.

Prior to computing Moran’s 𝐼, SOC values were standardized to 
zero mean and unit variance. This standardization ensures that the 
statistic reflects relative deviations from the global mean rather than 
absolute magnitudes, facilitates the interpretation of the Moran scatter 
plot, and allows the spatial lag to be expressed on a comparable scale.

Consequently, the slope of the regression line in the Moran scatter plot 
corresponds directly to the global Moran’s 𝐼 coefficient.

The spatial weights matrix was constructed using a 𝑘-nearest neigh-
bors approach (𝑘= 3) based on Haversine distances between sampling 
locations. Weights were defined as the inverse of the inter-point dis-
tance and row-standardized so that the spatial lag corresponds to a 
weighted local average of neighboring SOC values.

Statistical significance was evaluated using a Monte Carlo per-
mutation test with 999 random permutations of the observed SOC 
values. Under the null hypothesis of spatial randomness, SOC values are 
assumed to be spatially independent conditional on the specified spatial 
weights matrix. The observed global Moran’s 𝐼 value was 𝐼= −0.065, 
with a permutation-based 𝑝-value of 𝑝= 0.179. Therefore, the null 
hypothesis could not be rejected at the 𝛼= 0.05 significance level, 
indicating no statistically significant global spatial autocorrelation of 
SOC.

Fig. 5 presents the Moran scatter plot, which provides a complemen-
tary graphical interpretation of this result. The near-zero and slightly 
negative slope of the regression line indicates a very weak inverse 
association between SOC values and the average SOC of neighboring 
locations. The wide dispersion of points across the four quadrants 
further suggests that local deviations from the global mean are not 
systematically aligned with their spatial context, consistent with a 
largely random spatial structure at the analyzed scale.

To further investigate potential localized spatial patterns that may 
not be captured by the global statistic, Local Indicators of Spatial As-
sociation (LISA) were examined through a Moran quadrant map. LISA 
decomposes the global Moran’s 𝐼 into location-specific contributions, 
allowing the identification of local clusters (high–high and low–low) 
and spatial outliers (high–low and low–high). This local perspective is 
particularly relevant in heterogeneous environmental systems, where 
spatial dependence may manifest only in restricted areas rather than at 
the regional scale.

where 𝑧𝑖 denotes the standardized SOC value at location 𝑖, 𝑧𝑗 is the 
standardized SOC value at a neighboring location 𝑗, and 𝑤𝑖𝑗 represents 
the corresponding spatial weight. The local statistics 𝐼𝑖 quantify the 
contribution of each observation to the global Moran’s 𝐼 and allow the 
identification of local clusters and spatial outliers by jointly considering 
the sign of 𝑧𝑖 and its spatial lag.

Fig. 5. Moran scatter plot for SOC showing standardized SOC values versus 
their spatial lag. The slope of the fitted regression line corresponds to the 
global Moran’s 𝐼 statistic.

In Fig. 6 the LISA quadrant map reveals a spatially interspersed 
distribution of quadrant types, with no clearly delineated or spatially 
coherent clusters dominated by high–high or low–low associations. 
Instead, high and low SOC values frequently occur adjacent to con-
trasting neighbors, resulting in a substantial presence of spatial outliers. 
This pattern is indicative of pronounced local-scale heterogeneity and 
suggests that SOC variability is primarily governed by site-specific 
conditions rather than by smooth spatial gradients.

Taken together, the global Moran’s 𝐼 statistic, the Moran scatter 
plot, and the LISA quadrant map consistently indicate that SOC in 
the study area does not exhibit meaningful spatial autocorrelation at 
the examined scale, with variability largely characterized by localized 
patterns rather than by broad-scale spatial dependence.
